findings.explanation: encryptCredential() hard-codes the AES-256-GCM IV/nonce to 12 zero bytes on every call (line 32-33), and the key from deriveCredentialKey() is deterministic (SHA-256 of the single CREDENTIAL_MASTER_KEY env var, no per-record salt). This means every credential ever encrypted with this function uses the exact same (key, nonce) pair. Nonce reuse in GCM is catastrophic: it leaks the XOR of the plaintexts (letting an attacker with DB read access recover other stored page tokens once any one plaintext is known/guessed) and exposes the GHASH authentication subkey, enabling forged ciphertext/tags that decryptCredential() will accept as valid (the 'forbidden attack'). A fresh random IV must be generated per encryption (e.g. crypto.randomBytes(12)) — the envelope format already stores the IV alongside the ciphertext (line 39), so it just needs to actually be random.

Immediately after successfully decrypting a credential, resolvePageCredential() logs the plaintext secret (e.g. a Facebook page access token) to stdout. Since this function's entire purpose is to keep the secret encrypted at rest, writing it in cleartext to application logs (which are typically retained, shipped to log aggregators/monitoring, and readable by a wider audience than the credentials table) defeats the encryption and creates a persistent, easily-searchable copy of every secret. Drop ${secret} from the log line and log only non-sensitive identifiers (shop id, credential id).
